title: Help Students Remember the Right Answers by Asking for the Wrong Answers First
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer argues math education's decade-long push to destigmatize wrong answers has stayed mostly reactive -- posters promising mistakes are "expected, inspected, and corrected" if they appear -- when research suggests a more proactive approach works better. He centers on Sarah Shi Hui Wong's research, which had students copy a correct definition (Copy condition), copy a definition with a deliberately introduced and then struck-out error (Error-Cancel), or copy-and-then-correct that same deliberate error (Error-Correction); both error conditions outperformed simple copying on recall tests, and Wong's follow-up work ruled out effort as the explanation and found the error conditions also transferred better to new contexts. Meyer draws the practical implication that the problem space is full of wrong answers students could identify even when they can't yet produce the right one, and that teachers waste this resource by only ever asking for correct answers -- he suggests concrete moves like asking students for a number they know is too high or too low before finding an exact answer, or asking them to evaluate a non-solution point in a system of equations to connect the graph, equations, and solution space. He closes noting this reframing matters because right answers are a scarce resource held initially by few students, while wrong answers are a much more widely available one that teachers can turn into productive classroom material.
points: Wong's three-condition study (Copy, Error-Cancel, Error-Correction) found both conditions requiring students to deliberately generate and then address a wrong answer outperformed simple correct-definition copying on recall.
Follow-up experiments ruled out effort as the explanation for the effect and additionally found that deliberate-error conditions transferred better to new contexts than simple copying did.

Meyer's practical translation: ask students for a wrong answer before the right one -- a number they know is too high or too low, or a point that is deliberately not the solution to a system of equations -- to make use of knowledge students already have.

His closing framing reverses the usual scarcity logic of classroom answers: correct answers are held by few students at first, but wrong answers are abundant and available to nearly everyone, making them an underused teaching resource.
quotes: If the math education community has aligned on anything in the last ten years, it is the idea that students should not feel ashamed about their incorrect answers.
Recent research suggests we should consider wrong answers more proactively, effectively adding \"requested\" to those posters.
On tests of recall, the groups with deliberate errors performed significantly better than the group with errorless copying.
She also found in a later study that students in the \"error\" conditions were able to transfer their learning more readily to other contexts.
Many more students possess wrong answers and Wong’s research shows us how those answers, too, can be a resource for teachers.
Students who cannot find the precise solution of a system of equations can tell you a point that is not the precise solution.
